title: ReadyToRun and Native AOT by the numbers
cards/0/title: Three ways to get machine code
cards/0/body:
You already know three routes: the regular JIT, ReadyToRun (precompiled code next to the CIL) and Native AOT (the whole program ahead of time, no JIT). Now let us compare them on three axes:

  • startup — how long until the first useful action;
  • size — on disk and in memory;
  • peak speed — how fast hot code runs after warmup.

The fourth axis is what stops working. There is no universal winner: each option buys something and pays for it with something else.
cards/1/body:
Startup of a regular app: the host finds the runtime, the CLR initializes, assemblies load — and the JIT compiles every method on its first call. A web service has thousands of such methods, and JIT time can be a noticeable share of startup.

The .NET libraries themselves ship in ReadyToRun format, so the JIT mostly gets your code and generic instantiations. Exactly how much — you can ask the runtime.
cards/1/deep: JitInfo exists since .NET 6. From outside, dotnet-counters monitor shows the same: counters for compiled methods, IL bytes and time in the JIT from the System.Runtime provider. Good practice is to measure startup with these numbers before and after turning on ReadyToRun rather than take it on faith.
cards/2/q: An ASP.NET Core service starts slowly, and a noticeable part of startup is the JIT. The code uses reflection heavily and loads plugins from a folder. What should you try first?
cards/2/options/0: ReadyToRun: less JIT at startup and no restrictions
cards/2/options/1: Native AOT: startup will be the fastest
cards/2/explain: ReadyToRun is compatible with everything regular .NET can do: if the precompiled code is not enough, the JIT steps in. Native AOT cannot load plugins from a folder.
cards/2/wrong/1: Native AOT does not load assemblies on the fly, and reflection under it needs preparation. For this service it means a big rework.
cards/2/wrong/2: Without tiers every method is compiled fully optimized right away — startup gets slower.
cards/2/wrong/3: This attribute turns off tiers for the method: compilation is more expensive and there is no profile. It will not help startup.
cards/3/body:
R2R code is built ahead of time by the crossgen2 compiler, but it has to survive updates of the runtime and neighboring assemblies. Hence the limits:

  • methods from other assemblies cannot always be inlined: they may change after publishing;
  • the code targets a common instruction set, not the one the machine actually has;
  • there is no Dynamic PGO profile at build time.

So R2R code counts as the initial tier: it replaces Tier 0, and the JIT still recompiles hot methods into Tier 1. Startup is faster, peak speed is the same as with the regular JIT. The price is size: the file holds both CIL and machine code.
cards/3/deep:
The boundary within which inlining is allowed is called the version bubble. Composite R2R (PublishReadyToRunComposite, usually together with self-contained) compiles the app and the framework as one piece: the boundary is wider and more inlining happens, but you can no longer update the runtime separately.

Then and now: NGen in .NET Framework built images for a specific machine and framework version and regenerated them after every update. An R2R image is portable: if the code does not fit, the runtime simply discards it and calls the JIT.
cards/4/q: Why is ReadyToRun code usually slower than Tier 1 on the hot path? Select all.
cards/4/options/0: Methods from other assemblies are inlined with restrictions
cards/4/options/1: The code targets a common instruction set, not this processor
cards/4/options/2: There is no Dynamic PGO profile at build time
cards/4/options/3: An R2R file contains no CIL
cards/4/options/4: R2R code is run by an interpreter
cards/4/explain: That is exactly why hot R2R methods are recompiled into Tier 1. The file does contain CIL — without it recompilation would be impossible. There is no interpreter: R2R is ordinary machine code.
cards/5/title: Native AOT: the whole program ahead of time
cards/5/body:
The ILC compiler starts at Main, finds everything reachable, throws away the rest (trimming) and compiles to machine code. A small runtime goes alongside: the garbage collector, the type system, exception handling — no JIT. The result is a single executable for a single platform.

What it gives you:

  • startup — the fastest: no CIL to load, nothing to compile;
  • memory — less: no JIT, no JIT data structures, no Tier 0 code;
  • size — for a simple program on the order of a few megabytes, and .NET does not need to be installed.
cards/5/deep:
OptimizationPreference takes Speed or Size: a trade-off between code speed and file size. Native AOT builds for a specific RID; cross-compiling between operating systems is not supported.

Native AOT sees the whole program at once (closed world). If a class has no subclasses, the compiler can treat it as effectively sealed and call its methods directly. The JIT has no such knowledge: a new assembly with a subclass may load at any moment.
cards/6/q: Match the project property to what it does
cards/6/pairs/1/1: A single native file without a JIT
cards/6/pairs/4/1: The runtime ships with the app
cards/7/title: Peak speed: who leads after warmup
cards/7/body:
Native AOT starts fastest of all, but over a long run the JIT has its own trump cards:

  • the JIT knows the real processor and uses its instructions: checks like Vector256.IsHardwareAccelerated are constants for it;
  • the JIT has the Dynamic PGO profile and the values of static readonly fields.

Native AOT is built by default for a conservative instruction set and without a profile, but it is optimized from the start and sees the whole program. The qualitative summary:

  • startup: Native AOT < ReadyToRun < JIT;
  • peak speed: JIT ≈ ReadyToRun after warmup, Native AOT close — sometimes a bit lower, sometimes higher.

The peak difference is usually small and depends on the code — only a measurement on your own workload decides.
cards/7/deep: The instruction set for Native AOT is raised with the IlcInstructionSet property — but then the file will not run on processors without those instructions. The answer to "which is faster" changes from version to version: both the JIT and ILC improve noticeably in every .NET release, so old comparisons from the internet go stale.
cards/8/q: A service runs for weeks without restarts under constant load. Only peak throughput matters. What will most likely give the best result (and is worth checking with a measurement)?
cards/8/options/0: The regular JIT with tiers and Dynamic PGO
cards/8/options/2: ReadyToRun with the JIT turned off
cards/8/options/3: A Debug build with the JIT
cards/8/explain: Startup does not matter here, and over a long run the JIT adapts to the processor and the load profile. Native AOT may turn out no worse — but its wins are primarily startup and memory.
cards/8/wrong/1: The strengths of Native AOT are startup, memory and not depending on an installed .NET. For peak speed over a long run the JIT has more data.
cards/8/wrong/2: You cannot turn off the JIT for an R2R app: it is needed for hot methods and for everything missing from the image.
cards/8/wrong/3: In Debug the JIT does not optimize at all.
cards/9/title: The price of Native AOT: what stops working
cards/9/body:
The Native AOT world is closed: everything that will run must be known at build time. Therefore:

  • you cannot load a new assembly (Assembly.LoadFrom) or generate code (Reflection.Emit);
  • reflection over members that nothing in the code references may not find them — trimming cut them out;
  • Expression.Compile() works through an interpreter — slower.

The compiler warns you in advance: IL2xxx — trimming problems, IL3xxx — AOT problems. The cure is source generators: code that used to be built by reflection at run time is written at build time.
cards/9/deep: A library only needs <IsAotCompatible>true</IsAotCompatible> (.NET 8+): the trimming and AOT analyzers turn on, and warnings show up in a normal build rather than at the consumer. There are generators for System.Text.Json, regular expressions ([GeneratedRegex]), logging ([LoggerMessage]) and configuration binding.
cards/10/q: What works under Native AOT without rework? Select all.
cards/10/explain: LINQ is ordinary code, and generators write code at build time. Loading assemblies and Emit require a JIT, and Native AOT has none.
cards/11/q: A simple console app was published four ways. Order them from the smallest output to the largest.
cards/11/items/0: Framework-dependent .dll (the runtime is already on the machine)
cards/11/explain: Orders of magnitude: the .dll is kilobytes, but .NET must be installed; Native AOT is a few megabytes; self-contained with trimming is around ten megabytes; without trimming it is tens of megabytes, the whole runtime and libraries. Exact numbers depend on the version and the OS.
cards/12/q: Build Native AOT that puts code speed above file size
cards/12/explain: PublishAot turns on Native AOT, and OptimizationPreference=Speed asks ILC to prefer faster code even if the file ends up bigger.
